title: Literal types and const assertions (as const)
hook: A literal type is not just `string` — it is the exact value `"pending"` or `42`. Combined with `as const`, literals become the foundation for type-safe constants, discriminated unions, and configuration objects.

blocks.text: A **literal type** narrows a primitive to one specific value: `"circle"` instead of `string`, `200` instead of `number`, `true` instead of `boolean`. TypeScript infers literal types from `const` declarations automatically. **`as const`** (const assertion) freezes an entire object or array to its deepest literal values, making properties `readonly` and types exact. Literal unions like `"pending" | "done" | "failed"` replace enums in many modern codebases.

entries.plainDefinition: A type that allows only one specific string value.
A postfix assertion that tells TypeScript to infer the narrowest literal types and mark properties readonly.
When TypeScript expands a literal to its base type (e.g. `"hello"` → `string`) on `let` reassignment.
A union of object types sharing a common literal property (the discriminant) for safe narrowing.
entries.example: `{ kind: "circle"; r: number } | { kind: "square"; s: number }`

blocks.text: Literal types power discriminated unions — the most important pattern for modeling state machines, API responses, and Redux actions in TypeScript. Without `as const`, configuration objects widen to `string` and lose their exact keys. C# has `const` for compile-time constants but no literal type system — the closest analogue is enums or `nameof` string constants.

blocks.title: const vs as const
blocks.body: `const x = "ada"` infers the literal type `"ada"`. `const config = { port: 3000 }` widens to `{ port: number }`. Add `as const` to freeze the object: `{ readonly port: 3000 }`.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Build unions manually
items.body: `type Status = "pending" | "done" | "failed"` — a closed set of allowed strings.

items.title: Freeze with as const
items.body: `const ROUTES = { home: "/", about: "/about" } as const` — keys and values become readonly literals.

items.title: Derive types from values
items.body: `type Route = typeof ROUTES[keyof typeof ROUTES]` extracts `"/" | "/about"` from the object.

diagram.title: Literal type inference flow
diagram.source:
flowchart LR
  VAL["const x = 'pending'"] --> LIT["type: 'pending'"]
  LET["let x = 'pending'"] --> WIDE["type: string"]
  OBJ["{ port: 3000 }"] --> WOBJ["port: number"]
  AS["as const"] --> ROBJ["readonly port: 3000"]
  LIT --> UNION["'pending' | 'done'"]
  ROBJ --> DERIVE["typeof ROUTES[keyof typeof ROUTES]"]

snippet.label: const vs let widening
snippet.explanation: Line 1: `const` without reassignment keeps the literal type. Line 4: `let` widens to `string` because reassignment is allowed. Line 7: literal `const` cannot be reassigned to a different string.

snippet.label: as const for configuration objects
snippet.explanation: Lines 1–5: `as const` makes each value a literal number and the object readonly. Line 7: `keyof typeof` gets the keys, indexed access extracts the union of values. Line 10: readonly prevents mutation.

snippet.label: Discriminated union with literal discriminant
snippet.explanation: Lines 1–3: `status` is a literal discriminant — TypeScript narrows `result` in each case branch. Lines 5–9: after handling both literals, the switch is exhaustive. Adding a third status without a case triggers a `never` error (see any-unknown-never topic).

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Using `let` when you need a literal type — widen to `string`/`number`. Forgetting `as const` on config objects. Building huge literal unions manually instead of deriving from `as const`. Confusing `as const` with `const` keyword — they serve different purposes.

blocks.text: Literal types are the backbone of discriminated unions, Redux action types, and event handler maps. `as const` plus `satisfies` (TS 4.9+) lets you validate object shape while preserving literal inference. Tuple `as const` produces readonly tuples with exact element types — useful for route definitions and test fixtures. In interviews, prefer `as const` objects over enums for tree-shaking and no reverse-mapping surprises.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Single source of truth for values + types
Deep readonly can surprise mutation attempts
Not a drop-in for reverse mapping

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Not knowing the difference between const and as const. Unable to derive a union type from a const object. Saying literal types exist at run time.

interviewTakeaways: const infers literal types; let widens to string/number/boolean.
as const freezes objects and arrays to readonly literal types.
Derive unions with typeof OBJ[keyof typeof OBJ].
60s: Literals are exact values as types. as const for config. Build discriminated unions with literal discriminants. Prefer over enums for tree-shaking.
Follow-up: when would you use satisfies instead of as const?
commonPitfalls: Using let and wondering why the type widened to string.
Forgetting as const on configuration objects.
Strong answer: 'const keeps literals. as const deep-freezes objects. Derive unions from const objects for single source of truth.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: JavaScript `Object.freeze` prevents mutation at run time. TypeScript `as const` adds compile-time readonly and literal inference — both can be used together.
C# `const` is compile-time only for primitives. TypeScript literal types are type-level only. C# enums generate run-time objects; TS literal unions do not.
